questions.title: Which membrane component lets fat-soluble substances cross by simple diffusion
questions.question: Which structural feature of the cell membrane allows fat-soluble substances to pass through it directly?

explanations.A: Correct. The cell membrane's lipid component is phospholipid arranged as a bilayer, hydrophilic heads facing the aqueous solutions on either side and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails packed in the middle. A fat-soluble (lipid-soluble) substance dissolves directly in that hydrophobic core and diffuses straight across it without needing any protein channel or carrier. This is why lipid solubility, not molecular size alone, is the main predictor of how easily a substance crosses a plasma membrane by simple diffusion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Integral channel proteins span the bilayer to move ions and water, and carrier proteins move small polar molecules such as glucose; both exist because those hydrophilic substances cannot cross the hydrophobic lipid core unassisted. A fat-soluble substance needs no such assistance, so this route is not the one being tested here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The glycocalyx is the carbohydrate coat on the membrane's outer face, built for recognition and adhesion, not for transport. It sits on top of the bilayer rather than providing any pathway through it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral proteins sit on the cytoplasmic face of the membrane and form the cytoskeleton that gives the cell its shape and elasticity. They play no part in letting any substance, fat-soluble or otherwise, cross the membrane.

questions.learning_objective: State that the phospholipid bilayer's hydrophobic core, not any membrane protein or the glycocalyx, is what lets fat-soluble substances cross the cell membrane by simple diffusion.

questions.title: The cell coat's function
questions.question: What is the main function of the cell coat (glycocalyx) on the outer surface of the plasma membrane?

options.A: Anchoring the cytoskeleton to the inner membrane surface
options.C: Providing structural rigidity to the lipid bilayer

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anchoring the cytoskeleton is the job of peripheral membrane proteins on the cytoplasmic (inner) face; the cell coat sits on the opposite, outer face and has no cytoskeletal role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The membrane potential is set by ion gradients and channel/pump proteins, not by the carbohydrate coat. The glycocalyx has no electrical role.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rigidity is not the glycocalyx's function; it is a fuzzy, flexible surface layer of glycoprotein and glycolipid, not a structural scaffold for the bilayer.
explanations.D: Correct. The cell coat, or glycocalyx, is the carbohydrate-rich layer on the external face of the plasma membrane only, made of glycoprotein and glycolipid. It carries the cell's surface receptors and antigens, which is what lets one cell recognise, adhere to and communicate with another and lets the immune system tell self from non-self. This recognition-and-adhesion role, not any structural or electrical one, is the function tested here.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cell coat/glycocalyx's function is cell recognition and adhesion, carried out from the membrane's outer face only.

questions.title: What pinocytosis takes into the cell
questions.question: Pinocytosis is the process by which a cell takes in:

options.A: Large particulate matter such as bacteria
options.B: A specific ligand bound to a surface receptor
options.C: Membrane-bound secretory vesicles from the Golgi
options.D: Extracellular fluid together with its dissolved ions

explanations.A: Incorrect. Taking in large particulate matter such as bacteria or cell debris is phagocytosis, a distinct, larger-scale form of endocytosis carried out chiefly by macrophages and neutrophils, not pinocytosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Uptake of one specific ligand already bound to its own surface receptor is receptor-mediated endocytosis, which concentrates a particular molecule via coated pits rather than sampling fluid indiscriminately.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secretory vesicles budding from the Golgi apparatus move material out of the cell (exocytosis) or between organelles; they are not what pinocytosis brings in.
explanations.D: Correct. Pinocytosis ("cell drinking") is the non-selective uptake of extracellular fluid and whatever small solutes and ions are dissolved in it, taken in by small vesicles pinching off the plasma membrane. It is one of the membrane's three endocytic pathways alongside phagocytosis and receptor-mediated endocytosis, and it is distinguished from the other two by not being size-selective or receptor-specific. Because it samples the surrounding fluid indiscriminately, pinocytosis is the route by which a cell also drinks in whatever ions happen to be dissolved in that fluid.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish pinocytosis (non-selective fluid-phase uptake) from phagocytosis and receptor-mediated endocytosis.

questions.title: Cytoskeletal element forming the centriole
questions.question: Which cytoskeletal element is arranged as nine triplets to form a centriole?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Intermediate filaments are the supportive, tissue-specific cytoskeletal proteins (cytokeratin, vimentin, desmin, and so on); they form no part of the centriole's wall.
explanations.B: Correct. A centriole is a short cylindrical structure whose wall is built of nine bundles of three microtubules each - twenty-seven microtubules in total - with no membrane and no central pair. A pair of centrioles, surrounded by a tubulin matrix, forms the centrosome, the cell's microtubule-organising centre, which duplicates and moves to opposite poles to organise the mitotic spindle. Centrioles also template the basal bodies of cilia and flagella, which share the same nine-triplet microtubule structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Actin microfilaments are the thinnest cytoskeletal element, involved in cell motility and the terminal web beneath microvilli; they are not the building block of the centriole.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myosin thick filaments are a muscle-contraction protein, not a general cytoskeletal element, and play no part in centriole structure.

questions.learning_objective: State that a centriole is a cylinder of nine microtubule triplets, and that a pair of centrioles forms the centrosome that organises the mitotic spindle.

questions.title: Mutated protein impairing flagellar function
questions.question: Mutation of which protein would most directly impair flagellar function in sperm?

explanations.A: Correct. The flagellum's motile core (axoneme) is built of microtubules, themselves polymers of the protein tubulin, arranged in the classic 9+2 pattern with dynein arms that slide the microtubule doublets past each other to produce the beat. A mutation impairing tubulin's ability to polymerise or interact with dynein would directly cripple this microtubule-based motile machinery. The centriole that templates the flagellum's basal body is itself built of tubulin-based microtubule triplets, underscoring how central this one protein is to ciliary and flagellar structure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Actin is the core protein of microvilli and of the cell's contractile/motility machinery elsewhere, but it is not the structural protein of the flagellar axoneme, which is microtubule- (tubulin-) based.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Keratin is an intermediate filament protein providing structural support in epithelial cells; it plays no part in flagellar motility.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Collagen is an extracellular connective-tissue fibre protein, entirely unrelated to the intracellular microtubule machinery that powers a flagellum.

questions.learning_objective: State that flagellar (and ciliary) motility depends on tubulin-based microtubules, the same protein family that builds the centriole.

questions.title: Immunohistochemical marker of a neuroglial tumour
questions.question: A brain tumour of neuroglial (astrocytic) origin is expected to stain positive on immunohistochemistry for which intermediate filament protein?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Desmin is the intermediate filament of muscle cells; a tumour staining positive for desmin points to a muscle-derived (myogenic) origin, not a glial one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cytokeratin is the intermediate filament of epithelium; it would mark a carcinoma of epithelial origin, not a tumour arising from glial cells.
explanations.C: Correct. Each tissue expresses its own intermediate filament protein, and glial cells express glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Because a tumour's cells retain the intermediate filament typical of the tissue they arose from, immunohistochemical staining for GFAP identifies a tumour of neuroglial (astrocytic) origin, distinguishing it from tumours of epithelial, muscle or mesenchymal origin. This tissue-specific staining is exactly why intermediate filament typing is used diagnostically to trace an unknown tumour back to its cell of origin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vimentin is the intermediate filament of connective tissue and muscle; it marks a mesenchymal, not a neuroglial, tumour.

questions.learning_objective: State that GFAP is the tissue-specific intermediate filament of glial cells, used by immunohistochemistry to identify a neuroglial tumour.

questions.title: Immunohistochemical marker of a mesenchymal tumour
questions.question: A soft-tissue tumour of mesenchymal origin is expected to stain positive on immunohistochemistry for which intermediate filament protein?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neurofilaments are the intermediate filament of neurons; they would mark a tumour of neuronal origin, not a mesenchymal one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cytokeratin marks epithelial-derived tumours (carcinomas); a mesenchymal tumour, which arises from connective tissue or muscle precursors, does not carry it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GFAP is the glial cell marker, used to identify tumours arising from neuroglia in the brain, not from mesenchymal tissue.
explanations.D: Correct. Vimentin is the intermediate filament expressed by cells of connective tissue and muscle - the mesenchymal lineage. Because a tumour's cells continue to express the intermediate filament characteristic of their tissue of origin, immunohistochemical staining for vimentin identifies a tumour as mesenchymal in origin, as opposed to epithelial (cytokeratin), neuronal (neurofilament) or glial (GFAP). This is the same tissue-specific-filament logic tested from the glial side in the GFAP question.

questions.learning_objective: State that vimentin is the tissue-specific intermediate filament of mesenchymal cells, used by immunohistochemistry to identify a mesenchymal tumour.

questions.title: Shape of mitochondrial DNA
questions.question: Mitochondrial DNA differs from nuclear DNA in that it is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mitochondrial DNA is not linear, and it is not paternally inherited; sperm mitochondria are essentially excluded from the zygote, so this option is wrong on both counts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mitochondrial DNA is circular, not linear; biparental inheritance is also wrong, since only the mother's mitochondria (from the ovum) populate the zygote.
explanations.C: Correct. Human mitochondrial DNA is a small, double-stranded circular supercoil, unlike the linear DNA of the nucleus, and it encodes the ribosomal RNAs, transfer RNAs and proteins needed chiefly for oxidative phosphorylation. Because the oocyte supplies essentially all of the zygote's mitochondria, mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother, which is why it is used to trace maternal lineage. This combination of a circular genome with strictly maternal transmission is unique to mitochondrial DNA among the cell's genetic material.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The circular shape is right, but inheritance is not biparental; it is exclusively maternal, since mitochondria are supplied by the ovum and essentially not by sperm.

questions.learning_objective: State that mitochondrial DNA is a small circular molecule, inherited only from the mother.

questions.title: Face of the Golgi apparatus that buds transport vesicles
questions.question: Which face of the Golgi apparatus buds off the vesicles that carry its finished products onward?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cis face is the entry face: it is where transfer vesicles arriving from the rough endoplasmic reticulum are received, not where finished products leave.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Golgi has no "nuclear face" as a named structural pole; its two named faces are cis (entry) and trans (exit).
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Lateral face" is not one of the Golgi's two named functional poles either; only cis and trans are recognised.
explanations.D: Correct. The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened, curved saccules with two distinct faces: the cis (entry) face receives transfer vesicles from the rough endoplasmic reticulum, while the trans (exit) face buds off the finished products - secretory vesicles, lysosomes and coated vesicles. Everything the Golgi packages for export or delivery elsewhere in the cell therefore leaves specifically from the trans face. Mixing up a transfer vesicle (a Golgi input at the cis face) with a Golgi product (which buds from the trans face) is the most common way this distinction is tested.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Golgi apparatus's trans (exit) face, not its cis (entry) face, is where its products bud off.

questions.title: Organelle synthesising steroid hormones
questions.question: A cell specialised for steroid hormone synthesis is expected to be rich in which organelle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes, is abundant in cells that export protein (such as plasma cells), not in cells making steroid hormones.
explanations.B: Correct. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a membranous organelle specialised for lipid and steroid synthesis, and it is well developed in cells that make fat and steroid hormones, such as adrenal cortical and gonadal cells and hepatocytes. On light microscopy it is not seen directly, but its abundance produces the characteristic cytoplasmic acidophilia of steroid-secreting cells. On electron microscopy it appears as a network of branching, anastomosing, ribosome-free tubules continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus packages and modifies secretory products for export but is not itself the site of steroid synthesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peroxisomes carry out fatty-acid beta-oxidation and hydrogen peroxide detoxification, not steroid hormone synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: State that smooth endoplasmic reticulum, not rough ER or the Golgi, is the organelle specialised for lipid and steroid hormone synthesis.

questions.title: Light-microscopic appearance of smooth endoplasmic reticulum
questions.question: On light microscopy, an abundance of smooth endoplasmic reticulum in a cell's cytoplasm is recognised by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Basophilia from bound ribosomes is the light-microscopic signature of rough, not smooth, endoplasmic reticulum - smooth ER carries no ribosomes at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The negative Golgi image (an unstained region beside the nucleus on H&E) identifies the Golgi apparatus, a separate organelle from smooth ER.
explanations.C: Correct. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is not itself demonstrated by any routine light-microscopic stain, since it is a ribosome-free network of anastomosing tubules with no bound dye-binding component of its own. Where it is abundant, however, it produces a distinctive cytoplasmic acidophilia (eosinophilia), which is how its presence is inferred on light microscopy - for example in steroid-secreting cells. On electron microscopy it is confirmed directly as branching, ribosome-free tubules continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coarse azurophilic granules describe a feature of certain white blood cells (such as the primary granules of neutrophils or lymphocytes), unrelated to smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.learning_objective: State that smooth endoplasmic reticulum is inferred on light microscopy by the cytoplasmic acidophilia it produces, since the organelle itself is not directly stained.

questions.title: Peroxisome enzymes and the paper's thermoregulation key
questions.question: The peroxisome's oxidase enzymes carry out beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids, generating hydrogen peroxide as a by-product (broken down by the peroxisome's own catalase). Which of the following is this beta-oxidation reaction's other, non-toxic by-product, and the reason the paper's own key names the peroxisome an organelle 'responsible for maintaining body temperature'?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peroxisomal beta-oxidation does not conserve its energy as ATP the way mitochondrial beta-oxidation does; the reaction is not coupled to oxidative phosphorylation, so ATP synthesis is not its product.
explanations.B: Correct. Peroxisomes hold oxidase enzymes that carry out beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids, and unlike mitochondrial beta-oxidation this reaction is not coupled to ATP synthesis - its chemical energy is released as heat instead, with hydrogen peroxide as a toxic by-product that the peroxisome's own catalase then breaks down. This heat-releasing, uncoupled fatty-acid oxidation is the basis for the paper's own printed key naming the peroxisome as involved in maintaining body temperature. The classically taught, more specific thermoregulatory organelle is brown-fat mitochondrial oxidation via uncoupling protein (this same paper tests that separately as its own item), but the peroxisome's oxidase reaction is directionally consistent with a heat-generating role, and the printed key is recorded here as given rather than corrected.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lactate is the product of anaerobic glycolysis in the cytoplasm, unrelated to peroxisomal fatty-acid oxidation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bile salts are synthesised from cholesterol in the liver via a separate pathway; they are not a by-product of the peroxisome's oxidase reaction.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that peroxisomal fatty-acid oxidation releases its energy as heat rather than ATP, which is the textbook basis for the source paper's own printed key linking the peroxisome to body-temperature maintenance, while noting that brown-fat mitochondria are the more specific classical answer for thermoregulation.

questions.title: Chromosome number of the cells produced at telophase I of meiosis
questions.question: At the end of telophase I of meiosis, each of the two daughter cells contains:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 46 single-chromatid chromosomes describes neither product of meiosis I; the chromosome number is already halved by telophase I, and the chromatids are not yet split.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 23 is the right chromosome number, but the chromosomes are still double-chromatid (d) at this stage; splitting into single chromatids (s) does not happen until anaphase II, the second meiotic division.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 46 double-chromatid chromosomes describes the starting cell's own state after DNA replication, before meiosis I has separated the homologous pairs; it is not what remains in each daughter cell afterward.
explanations.D: Correct. Meiosis I is the reduction division: anaphase I separates the 23 bivalent (paired homologous) chromosomes to opposite poles, and telophase I yields two daughter cells, each with 23 double-chromatid (d) chromosomes - the haploid chromosome number, but with each chromosome still made of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Those sister chromatids are only split apart, producing single-chromatid (s) chromosomes, during anaphase of the second, mitosis-like meiotic division. This halving of chromosome number at meiosis I, with the chromatid count staying at two until meiosis II, is what makes meiosis I the true reduction division.

questions.learning_objective: State that telophase I of meiosis yields two daughter cells each with 23 double-chromatid chromosomes, and distinguish this from the single-chromatid, still-46 or already-23 states at other points in mitosis and meiosis.

questions.title: Cell-population category of smooth muscle
questions.question: By its capacity for renewal, smooth muscle is classified as a:

options.D: Population with no defined renewal capacity

explanations.A: Incorrect. A static (permanent) population is made of end cells that have left the cell cycle for good and are never replaced, such as the neuron and the cardiac muscle cell. Smooth muscle cells retain the ability to divide, so this does not describe them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A renewing (labile) population is continuously lost and continuously replaced from stem cells, as in blood, epidermis and gut lining. Smooth muscle is not being constantly turned over this way.
explanations.C: Correct. Cell populations are grouped by whether their cells can re-enter the cell cycle. A potentially renewable (stable) population, unlike a renewing one, sits in a resting phase and is not dividing under ordinary conditions, but its cells retain the ability to come back into the cycle and divide when replacement or growth demands it - the liver cell and the fibroblast after injury are the classic examples, and smooth muscle behaves the same way, dividing on demand (for example during vascular injury or pregnancy) rather than continuously. This on-demand, reversible capacity is what separates a stable/potentially renewable population from both the never-dividing static population and the continuously dividing renewing population.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renewal capacity is a defined, examinable property for every tissue; smooth muscle specifically falls into the potentially renewable (stable) category rather than being an exception with no defined category.

questions.learning_objective: Classify smooth muscle as a potentially renewable (stable) cell population, and distinguish this category from static (permanent) and renewing (labile) populations.

questions.title: Macrophage nucleus shape
questions.question: On light microscopy, the nucleus of a macrophage is best described as:

options.A: A small, dense, centrally placed round nucleus
options.D: A basophilic nucleus with a clock-face chromatin pattern

explanations.A: Incorrect. A small, dense, central round nucleus describes a resting lymphocyte, not the larger, irregular macrophage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A large, pale, multilobed nucleus describes a neutrophil or another multinucleated/lobulated cell, not the macrophage's single kidney-shaped nucleus.
explanations.C: Correct. The macrophage is a large, irregular connective-tissue cell derived from the blood monocyte, with pale basophilic cytoplasm and a characteristic dark, kidney (reniform) shaped nucleus placed eccentrically within the cell. It is specifically demonstrated with a vital stain such as trypan blue or India ink, which the cell phagocytoses, leaving visible dye granules in its cytoplasm as confirmation. This eccentric, kidney-shaped nucleus is the single most useful feature for identifying a macrophage on a routine section.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A "clock-face" chromatin pattern around the nuclear rim describes the plasma cell's nucleus, a different connective-tissue cell entirely.

questions.title: Epithelium lining a surface exposed to wear and tear
questions.question: A wet surface subjected to constant mechanical wear and tear, such as the oesophagus, is normally lined by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple columnar epithelium, a single layer of tall cells, is suited to secretion and absorption (as in the gut lining) rather than resisting surface abrasion; a single cell layer offers little protection against friction.
explanations.B: Correct. Stratified squamous epithelium is many layers thick - typically 5 to 30 - built from columnar basal cells that flatten progressively toward the free surface, with the surface cells joined by desmosomes. Where it lines a wet internal surface subject to mechanical wear, such as the oesophagus, oral cavity or vagina, it stays non-keratinised, in contrast to the keratinised form that covers the dry external skin. This many-layered, desmosome-bound structure is exactly what gives it its protective role against friction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transitional epithelium is specific to the urinary tract, where its distension-dependent layering suits the bladder's stretch, not a surface whose main demand is resisting wear from a passing bolus or friction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is specialised for moving fluid or particles across its surface (as in the respiratory tract), not for withstanding mechanical abrasion.

questions.learning_objective: State that a wet surface subject to wear and tear is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium, distinguishing it from the keratinised (skin) form and from simple, transitional and pseudostratified epithelia.

questions.title: Transitional epithelium in the empty bladder
questions.question: In an empty (undistended) urinary bladder, transitional epithelium is:

options.A: 3-4 layers thick with flattened superficial cells
options.B: A single layer of dome-shaped cells
options.C: 6-8 layers thick with dome-shaped superficial cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. 3-4 layers with flattened superficial cells describes the full, distended bladder, where the epithelium thins and its cells are pushed laterally - the opposite state to the one asked about here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transitional epithelium is never a single layer; it is a stratified epithelium (6-8 layers empty, thinning to 3-4 full).
explanations.C: Correct. Transitional epithelium (urothelium), which lines the renal pelvis, ureter, bladder and prostatic urethra, is 6 to 8 layers thick in the empty bladder. Its dome-shaped superficial cells have a convex luminal surface covered by rigid membrane plaques that act as a urine-impermeable barrier, and are sometimes binucleated. As the bladder fills, the intermediate cells are pushed laterally and the whole epithelium thins to only 3-4 layers, with the superficial cells flattening - this distension-dependent change in layer count and cell shape is the epithelium's defining feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transitional epithelium is not keratinised anywhere in the urinary tract, and it does not reach 10 or more layers even at its thickest (empty) state.

questions.learning_objective: State that transitional epithelium is 6-8 layers thick with dome-shaped superficial cells in the empty bladder, thinning to 3-4 layers with flattened cells when the bladder is full.

questions.title: Apical surface specialisation lining the epididymis
questions.question: The pseudostratified epithelium lining the epididymis carries which apical surface specialisation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Motile cilia with a microtubular axoneme mark the ciliated respiratory epithelium (and the uterine tube), a different pseudostratified epithelium from the one lining the epididymis; the epididymis's apical processes cannot beat.
explanations.B: Correct. The pseudostratified epithelium of the male genital tract, notably the epididymis, carries stereocilia: long, often clumped apical processes that, despite the name, are actually a specialised form of microvillus, not a true cilium. They share a microvillus's actin core rather than a cilium's microtubular axoneme, so they cannot beat, and the epithelium bearing them lacks the goblet cells of the ciliated respiratory variety. This wording (stereocilia, epididymis) reflects the anatomically coherent version of the fact; a second sitting of this same exam paper miswrote the site as "epidermis" while keeping the identical correct answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A plain striated/microvillous brush border of short, uniform microvilli (without the long, clumped stereocilia) is the specialisation of absorptive epithelium such as the small intestine and kidney tubule, not the epididymis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epididymis's epithelium does carry a defined apical specialisation - stereocilia - it is not a plain, unspecialised apical surface.

questions.learning_objective: Identify stereocilia as the apical specialisation of the epididymis's pseudostratified epithelium, and distinguish them from true motile cilia by their microvillus-type actin core.

questions.title: The goblet cell as a unicellular gland
questions.question: The goblet cell is an example of which class of exocrine gland?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A multicellular compound gland has a branched duct system serving many secretory units; the goblet cell is a single cell, not a multicellular structure with any duct at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A multicellular simple gland still has more than one secretory cell, typically opening by a single unbranched duct; the goblet cell has neither multiple cells nor a duct.
explanations.C: Correct. By number of secretory cells, an exocrine gland is either unicellular (a single cell) or multicellular. The goblet cell is the classic unicellular example: one flask-shaped, mucus-secreting cell scattered within the pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium of the respiratory tract and the simple columnar epithelium of the intestine. It needs no duct, because sitting directly within the surface epithelium already puts its secretion where it needs to go.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The goblet cell is exocrine, releasing mucus directly onto a free surface, not endocrine (which would mean secreting into the bloodstream with no surface or duct connection).

questions.learning_objective: Classify the goblet cell as a unicellular exocrine gland, needing no duct because it already sits within the surface epithelium.

questions.title: Epithelium lining the thyroid follicle
questions.question: The follicles of the thyroid gland are lined by which epithelium?

explanations.A: Correct. Simple cuboidal epithelium is a single layer of cells as tall as they are wide, each with a central rounded nucleus, and it lines the thyroid follicles as well as the secretory acini of glands and the kidney's convoluted tubules. Its functions - secretion and reabsorption - fit the thyroid follicular cell's dual role of secreting thyroglobulin into the follicular lumen and later reabsorbing it for hormone release. This single-cell-layer, cuboidal shape is the identifying feature on a thyroid section.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of flat cells suited to diffusion and filtration (as in alveoli or capillary walls), not the secretion-and-reabsorption role of the thyroid follicular cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stratified cuboidal epithelium is more than one cell layer thick and lines structures such as sweat gland ducts; the thyroid follicle is lined by a single layer, not a stratified one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Simple columnar epithelium is taller than it is wide, suited to absorption along the gut; the thyroid follicular cell is cuboidal, not columnar, in its normal resting state.

questions.learning_objective: State that the thyroid follicle is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, matching its secretory-and-reabsorptive function.

questions.title: What epithelial polarity facilitates in an absorptive cell
questions.question: The apical microvilli of a polarised absorptive epithelial cell chiefly facilitate:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cell-to-cell adhesion is the job of lateral junctions such as the zonula adherens and desmosome, not of apical microvilli.
explanations.B: Correct. A microvillus is a finger-like projection of the apical cell surface with a core of actin filaments anchored into the cytoskeleton's terminal web, shorter than a cilium and containing no microtubules. Their combined mass, seen by light microscopy as a striated or brush border, greatly increases the apical surface area available for absorption, which is why they are dense on absorptive epithelia such as the small intestine lining and the kidney's proximal convoluted tubule. This apical polarity - concentrating absorptive machinery specifically at the luminal surface - is what lets a polarised epithelial cell absorb fluid and nutrients efficiently from the lumen it faces.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Basal ion pumping is powered by basal infoldings and the mitochondria packed between them, a feature of the cell's opposite (basal), not apical, pole.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mechanical protection against friction is provided by a thick, many-layered stratified squamous epithelium, not by microvilli on a simple absorptive epithelium.

questions.learning_objective: State that apical microvilli increase surface area to facilitate absorption, as part of the general principle that epithelial polarity places specialised structures where their function is needed.

questions.title: Basal infoldings and ion-transporting cells
questions.question: Basal membrane infoldings, with mitochondria packed vertically between them, are a feature of which type of cell?

options.B: An ion-transporting cell such as a kidney tubule cell
options.C: A ciliated cell specialised for particle transport

explanations.A: Incorrect. Basal infoldings are a specialised, energy-demanding feature; a resting, non-secretory cell has no particular need for the increased basal surface area and packed mitochondria they provide.
explanations.B: Correct. Basal infoldings are invaginations of the basal cell membrane that increase the basal surface area available for transport, with mitochondria arranged vertically in the compartments between the folds to supply energy for active transport on the spot. This combination is characteristic of ion-transporting cells, of which the standard example is the kidney tubule cell, whose job is to actively reclaim ions from the filtrate across its basal membrane into the interstitium. The tight local pairing of transport surface and ATP supply is exactly what an energetically demanding, continuous ion-pumping job requires.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A ciliated cell's specialisation - motile cilia with a microtubular axoneme - is at its apical, not basal, surface, and serves particle transport across the surface rather than basal ion transport.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The goblet cell's specialisation is apical mucus secretion; it has no particular basal infolding feature.

questions.learning_objective: State that basal infoldings, packed with mitochondria, increase surface area to power active ion transport, characteristic of cells such as the kidney tubule cell.

questions.title: Intercellular junction anchoring intermediate filaments (cytokeratin)
questions.question: Which epithelial cell junction anchors bundles of intermediate filaments (cytokeratin/tonofilaments) on its cytoplasmic side?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The zonula occludens fuses adjacent membranes to seal the intercellular space; it anchors no cytoplasmic filament system at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The gap junction is a communicating channel, not an anchoring junction, and has no cytoplasmic attachment plaque or associated filament system.
explanations.C: Correct. Both adherens-type junctions bridge a wide intercellular space with calcium-dependent transmembrane proteins, but they differ in what they anchor on the cytoplasmic side. The macula adherens, or desmosome, does not encircle the cell like a belt - it is scattered as discrete, disc-shaped spots, each with a thickened cytoplasmic attachment plaque into which bundles of intermediate filaments (cytokeratin in epithelium, called tonofilaments) are anchored. This cytokeratin anchorage is what makes the desmosome the strongest of the junctions, which is why it is abundant between the cells of stratified squamous epithelium, where the surface is subjected to friction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The zonula adherens encircles the cell like a belt and anchors actin filaments, not intermediate filaments, on its cytoplasmic side - the opposite pairing from the desmosome.

questions.learning_objective: State that the desmosome (macula adherens), not the zonula adherens, tight junction or gap junction, anchors cytokeratin/intermediate filament bundles, and is therefore the strongest junction where surfaces meet friction.

questions.title: The tight junction as a paracellular barrier
questions.question: Which lateral cell junction restricts the passage of substances between adjacent epithelial cells, forcing them to cross through the cells instead?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The gap junction is the one junction that lets material pass directly between cells through its channels; it is a communicating, not a barrier, junction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The desmosome's role is mechanical adhesion (anchoring intermediate filaments) against friction, not sealing the paracellular space against substance passage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The zonula adherens provides lateral adhesion via actin anchorage across a wide intercellular space; it does not fuse the membranes or seal that space.
explanations.D: Correct. The zonula occludens, or tight/occluding junction, is the most apical of the lateral junctions. The two adjacent plasma membranes actually fuse at points through transmembrane proteins contributed by each cell, obliterating the intercellular space at those points and encircling the apex of the cell like a belt. This seal restricts the passage of substances between adjacent cells - it makes the epithelium a true barrier rather than a sieve, forcing anything crossing it to pass through the cells (transcellular route) rather than between them (paracellular route).

questions.learning_objective: State that the zonula occludens (tight junction) is the barrier junction that fuses adjacent membranes and forces molecules to cross an epithelium transcellularly rather than paracellularly.

questions.title: Protein subunit of a gap junction channel
questions.question: Each channel of a gap junction, through which ions and small molecules pass directly between adjacent cells, is built of how many transmembrane protein subunits (a connexon)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Four subunits is not the connexon count; the correct number is six per hemichannel.
explanations.B: Correct. The gap junction, or nexus, is the one lateral junction through which material actually passes between cells: the gap between the two membranes is narrow and bridged by channels, each built of six symmetrical transmembrane protein subunits (a connexon), through which ions and small molecules move directly from the interior of one cell to the interior of the next. Between muscle cells, the same channels carry electrical impulses, which is how cardiac and smooth muscle cells contract as a functional syncytium. Unlike the other three lateral junctions, the gap junction is not part of the junctional complex, since its role is communication rather than adhesion or sealing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eight subunits is not the connexon count for a gap junction channel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Twelve would be the total across a full, paired channel spanning both cells (two connexons of six each), but the subunit count of a single connexon - the actual figure this question asks for - is six, not twelve.

questions.learning_objective: State that a gap junction channel (connexon) is built of six transmembrane protein subunits, and that the gap junction alone among the lateral junctions actually lets material pass between cells.

questions.title: Hemidesmosome function
questions.question: The hemidesmosome, on the basal surface of basal epithelial cells, functions to:

options.A: Anchor the epithelial cytoskeleton to the underlying basement membrane
options.B: Seal the paracellular space against solute passage
options.C: Provide a channel for direct cell-to-cell communication
options.D: Join adjacent basal cells to each other

explanations.A: Correct. Every epithelium rests on a basement membrane, itself made of an epithelial basal lamina (type IV collagen and glycoproteins) and an underlying connective-tissue reticular lamina (type III collagen and ground substance). Hemidesmosomes - shaped like half a desmosome - sit on the basal surface of the basal cells and fix the epithelium down onto this basement membrane, anchoring the epithelial cytoskeleton to it. This anchorage, together with the basement membrane's own filtration role at sites like the kidney glomerulus and lung alveolus, is what gives the epithelium-connective tissue interface both support and controlled permeability.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sealing the paracellular space is the tight junction's (zonula occludens) role, a lateral junction between neighbouring cells, not the hemidesmosome's role at the basal surface toward the basement membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Direct cell-to-cell communication is the gap junction's function; the hemidesmosome connects a cell to the basement membrane below it, not to a neighbouring cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Joining adjacent basal cells to each other is done by lateral junctions such as the desmosome, between two cell membranes; the hemidesmosome instead anchors one cell to the extracellular basement membrane beneath it, which is why it is only "half" a desmosome.

questions.learning_objective: State that the hemidesmosome anchors the epithelial cytoskeleton to the underlying basement membrane, distinguishing it from lateral junctions that connect neighbouring cells to each other.

questions.title: Connective tissue fibre forming delicate supporting networks
questions.question: Which connective tissue fibre branches and anastomoses into a delicate supporting network for the cells of an organ's stroma?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Collagen type I is the strongest, most abundant fibre, giving tensile strength to structures like tendon and the dermis; it forms thick bundles, not a delicate branching network.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Elastic fibres allow stretch and recoil, as needed in a large artery wall; their job is elasticity, not forming a delicate supportive stromal network.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibronectin is a ground-substance glycoprotein that helps cells adhere to the extracellular matrix; it is not one of the three connective tissue fibres.
explanations.D: Correct. There are three connective tissue fibres, and each does one mechanical job. Reticular fibres, built of collagen type III, branch and anastomose into a loose, flexible, delicate network that supports the cells of an organ - which is exactly what "stroma" means. This is in contrast to collagen type I, which resists stretching in structures needing raw strength, and elastic fibres, which stretch and recoil in structures like the aorta.

questions.learning_objective: State that reticular fibres (collagen III) form the delicate, branching supportive network of an organ's stroma, distinguishing their role from collagen I's strength and elastic fibres' recoil.

questions.title: Dense connective tissue of tendons and ligaments
questions.question: The dense white fibrous connective tissue of tendons and ligaments, where collagen bundles run parallel in one direction, is classified as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen bundles interwoven in every plane to resist pull from multiple directions, as in the dermis or an organ capsule - not the single-direction parallel arrangement of a tendon.
explanations.B: Correct. Dense white fibrous connective tissue is packed with collagen bundles and holds few cells and little ground substance. It is regular when the bundles run parallel, all pulling in one direction, which is exactly the arrangement of tendons, ligaments and aponeuroses. This parallel bundle direction, following the single-direction pull the tissue must resist, is what distinguishes dense regular from dense irregular connective tissue, whose bundles instead interweave in multiple planes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mucoid connective tissue is a soft, jelly-like tissue rich in hyaluronic acid, found in sites like the umbilical cord and vitreous - structurally and functionally unrelated to the dense, collagen-packed tissue of a tendon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Loose areolar connective tissue is sparse in fibres and cell-poor by comparison, well vascularised and flexible - the opposite of the densely packed, low-cellularity tissue that gives a tendon its tensile strength.

questions.learning_objective: Classify tendon and ligament as dense regular connective tissue, whose collagen bundles run parallel in one direction, distinguishing it from dense irregular, mucoid and loose areolar connective tissue.

questions.title: Distinguishing feature of dense regular vs irregular connective tissue
questions.question: What distinguishes dense regular from dense irregular white fibrous connective tissue?

options.A: Only the regular form contains collagen
options.B: Only the irregular form resists any pulling force
options.C: The direction of the collagen bundles, following the direction of the pulling force
options.D: The regular form has abundant ground substance and few fibres

explanations.A: Incorrect. Both forms are built of densely packed collagen bundles; collagen content is not what separates them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both forms resist pulling force - that is the defining mechanical job of dense connective tissue generally; what differs is the direction from which each resists it.
explanations.C: Correct. Both dense regular and dense irregular connective tissue are packed with collagen bundles and hold few cells and little ground substance. The regular form has its bundles running parallel, resisting pull from one direction only, as in tendons, ligaments and aponeuroses; the irregular form has its bundles interwoven in multiple planes, resisting pull from any direction, as in the dermis, organ capsules, the periosteum and perichondrium, and mammary gland stroma. This bundle-direction difference follows directly from the direction of the force each tissue is built to withstand.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both forms hold little ground substance and few cells by definition (that is what makes them "dense"); this is not a point of difference between the regular and irregular forms, and it misdescribes the regular form specifically, which is collagen-dense, not ground-substance-rich.

questions.learning_objective: State that dense regular and dense irregular connective tissue are distinguished by collagen bundle direction, which follows the direction of the pulling force each is built to resist.

questions.title: Loose areolar connective tissue's cell and fibre content
questions.question: Which connective tissue proper is the most widespread type and the only one containing every connective tissue cell type and every fibre type together?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dense regular connective tissue is cell-poor and dominated by parallel collagen bundles specifically, not a mix of every fibre and cell type.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mucoid connective tissue is a specific, hyaluronic-acid-rich jelly found in restricted sites (umbilical cord, vitreous, dental pulp), not the widespread, all-inclusive tissue this question describes.
explanations.C: Correct. Loose areolar connective tissue is the most common and most widespread type of connective tissue proper, lying under nearly every epithelium and in nearly every space in the body. Unlike the other, more specialised connective tissue types, it contains every type of connective tissue cell and all three types of fibre, along with the most abundant ground substance of any connective tissue type. Its name comes from the areolae, potential spaces within it that can fill with fluid or gas, and it is flexible and well vascularised, which is why it also serves as the tissue most often examined first when learning the general connective tissue cell and fibre types.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reticular connective tissue is a specialised type dominated by reticular fibres and reticular cells specifically, forming the stroma of organs such as lymph nodes - it is not the mixed, all-cell-and-fibre-type tissue described here.

questions.title: Site of white (unilocular) adipose connective tissue
questions.question: White (unilocular) adipose connective tissue, made of fat cells each storing a single large lipid droplet, is found at which of the following sites?

options.A: Interscapular region of the newborn only
options.B: Behind the eyeball, in the orbit
options.D: Only in fetal life, disappearing after birth

explanations.A: Incorrect. The interscapular region in the newborn is the classic site of brown (multilocular), not white, adipose tissue.
explanations.B: Correct. White adipose connective tissue is made of unilocular fat cells - each storing fat as one large droplet - and is coloured white because it is poorly vascularised and its droplets contain carotenoids. It is affected by diet and hormones and lies both under the skin and around organs, including the padding behind the eyeball in the orbit, where it provides mechanical cushioning. This distribution under the skin, around organs and in protective spaces like the orbit is typical of white fat's structural and energy-storage role.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adipose tissue is not confined to red bone marrow; white fat is widespread subcutaneously and around organs throughout the body, including the orbit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. White fat is not restricted to fetal life; unlike brown fat, which is abundant in the fetus and newborn and is lost during childhood, white fat persists and in fact becomes the dominant adipose type through childhood and adulthood.

questions.learning_objective: State that white (unilocular) adipose tissue, unlike brown fat, is widespread in the adult, including at protective sites such as behind the eyeball.

questions.title: Consequence of absent brown fat in a newborn
questions.question: An infant born with an absence of brown (multilocular) adipose tissue is most likely to have impaired:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood clotting depends on the coagulation cascade and platelets, unrelated to brown adipose tissue.
explanations.B: Correct. Brown adipose tissue is made of multilocular fat cells and is coloured brown by its rich blood supply and by the cytochrome pigments of its unusually numerous mitochondria. It is abundant in fetal life and the newborn but is lost during childhood as it is progressively replaced by white fat, and its specific function is thermogenesis: its mitochondria burn fat to release heat directly via the uncoupling protein thermogenin, bypassing normal ATP synthesis. A newborn lacking brown fat is therefore left without this non-shivering thermogenesis mechanism, which is the newborn's chief defence against cold stress, since true shivering thermogenesis is not yet well developed at birth.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bilirubin conjugation is a hepatic (liver) enzymatic process, unrelated to adipose tissue of either type.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Passive immunity in the newborn comes from maternally transferred antibodies (largely IgG across the placenta), not from adipose tissue.

questions.learning_objective: State that brown adipose tissue's thermogenin-mediated, mitochondria-driven heat production is the newborn's non-shivering thermogenesis mechanism, so its absence impairs cold defence.

questions.title: Cell responsible for a bee-sting allergic reaction
questions.question: A local allergic reaction (itching, swelling, wheal) following a bee sting is chiefly mediated by degranulation of which connective tissue cell?

explanations.A: Correct. The mast cell's granules store heparin, histamine and serotonin, and it also releases eosinophil chemotactic factor and leukotrienes. Its surface carries IgE receptors, so that when an allergen - such as bee venom in a sensitised person - binds antibody already fixed to the cell, the granules discharge immediately. That discharge is the immediate allergic reaction: locally, itching, swelling and a wheal; systemically, in severe cases, anaphylactic shock from the same vasodilatation and increased permeability acting throughout the body.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The fibroblast is a protein-synthesising connective tissue cell responsible for laying down fibres and ground substance, not for mediating allergic reactions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The macrophage's role is phagocytosis of debris and pathogens and antigen presentation, not the immediate IgE-mediated degranulation response responsible for a bee-sting reaction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The plasma cell manufactures and secretes antibody but does not itself carry surface IgE receptors or degranulate in the way the mast cell does; it is basophilic like the mast cell but otherwise shares nothing functionally with it.

questions.learning_objective: State that the mast cell, via IgE-triggered degranulation of its histamine- and heparin-containing granules, mediates the immediate local allergic reaction to an insect sting.

questions.title: The fibrocyte's ability to return to an active state
questions.question: The inactive fibrocyte, unlike a fully differentiated end cell, retains which capability?

options.A: It can transform directly into a macrophage
options.B: It can re-enter an active, protein-synthesising fibroblast state when needed
options.D: It cannot participate in any repair process

explanations.A: Incorrect. A fibrocyte does not transform into a macrophage; macrophages derive from blood monocytes, an entirely separate cell lineage.
explanations.B: Correct. The fibroblast is the commonest cell of connective tissue proper, arising from the undifferentiated mesenchymal cell. In its active state it is a branched cell with deeply basophilic cytoplasm, a well-developed rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, and a euchromatic nucleus - the picture of a protein-synthesising cell. Its inactive form, the fibrocyte, is a smaller spindle cell with paler cytoplasm, more heterochromatin and less rER, Golgi and mitochondria, but critically it retains the ability to re-enter the active fibroblast state - for example after an injury - when new fibre and ground-substance synthesis is again required, which is exactly the reversible, on-demand behaviour of a potentially renewable (stable) cell population.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fibrocyte does not divide continuously and without stimulus; its division/reactivation is triggered on demand (such as by injury), not constant.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Far from being excluded from repair, the fibrocyte's defining feature is precisely its ability to reactivate and take part in repair by returning to the active, fibre-synthesising fibroblast state.

questions.learning_objective: State that the inactive fibrocyte retains the ability to re-enter the active, protein-synthesising fibroblast state on demand, such as after injury.
